text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.

- British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, on a visit to Stockholm, said he saw no barrier to Finland applying for NATO membership. Rifkind said he did not understand the view that monetary union had a security dimension.
- Airborne reconnaissance in the Baltic Sea region has picked up again after quiet period since the fall of the Soviet Union.
- Speaker of Parliament Riitta Uosukainen re-elected despite record number of protest votes.
- U.S. investor George Soros said that -- to his knowledge -- his funds had not speculated with the markka.
- New Eurostat rules for calculating state debt improve Finland's debt-to-GDP ratio.
- Finnish official Esko Kiuru appointed head of Moscow bureau of International Organisation for Migration.
- Eight radio stations seeking licences for nation-wide digital broadcasts.
- Snow church consecretated at Helsinki's Senate Square.
- Helsinki telephone operator Helsingin Puhelin Oy starts test use of technology which enables high quality video transmission in telephone networks.

- Aktia Bank will strengthen its position on the financial markets if it buys brokerage Oy Erik Selin Ab, as agreed in letter of intent. Selin has falling profits and would gain from Aktia's stronger balance sheet and distribution channels.

- Finnish participation in the EU's Technical Assistance to Commonwealth of Independent States (Tacis) aid programme to former Soviet Union states is strong, involving 70 to 80 companies, Tacis director Timo Summa says.
- Sawn goods prices are beginning to rise and export prices per cubic metres have been above 1,000 markka per cubic metre in this year's early deliveries, industry says.
- Some 2,000 demonstrators gathered in front of parliament on Monday to protest against a proposed law to allow shops to stay open on Sundays.
